deep.reconstruction:
There are no mathematical derivations on this page. It is a philosophical text, part of Riemann's critical discussion of G. T. Fechner's thesis (Zend-Avesta, 1851) that the Earth is an ensouled being (Erdseele). The argument runs as follows.

(0) Summary of Fechner. Fechner argues by analogy: the similarities between the Earth and ourselves point to the Earth being ensouled, and the dissimilarities point to its being a soul far higher than ours. Riemann judges that Fechner's persuasive force lies in the vivid, detailed overall picture, which makes up for the lack of rigour in the individual inferences. He therefore declines to summarise Fechner's line of argument. He will consider only its factual content and will rely on 'exact methods', namely induction of general laws and their use in explaining nature.

(1) Criterion for ensoulment. 'Ensouled' is defined as the occurrence of a continuing, unified thought-process (einheitlicher Denkprocess) in a being. We are directly certain of our own ensoulment. For other men and animals we infer it from individual purposive motions.

(2) Principle of explanation. Wherever perceived purposiveness is traced to a cause, the cause is sought in a thought-process; no other explanation is available. Riemann holds thought to be a process inside ponderable matter. He thinks it cannot be explained by spatial motions of matter, but concedes a remote possibility of such an explanation.

(3) Scope. Only conditioned ends are at issue, i.e. those bounded in time and space. Unconditioned ends are explained by an eternal Willing, not by a thought-process. The only purposiveness whose cause we directly perceive is that of our own actions: willing the ends and deliberating on the means.

(4) Inductive rule. Suppose a body of ponderable matter contains a closed system of ongoing end/means (Zweck- und Werkzeug-) relations. Then a continuing unified thought-process in that body is a possible explanation. It is the most probable one if both of the following hold:
(i) the purposiveness is not already completed in the germ (Keim) of the body;
(ii) there is no reason to seek its cause in a larger whole to which the body belongs.

(5) Application to men, animals and plants. Part of their purposiveness comes from an internal thought-process. Organic purposiveness, the design of the organism itself, comes from a thought-process in a larger whole. Three reasons are given:
1) Organic purposiveness is not closed within the single organism. The reasons for the human organism's design lie in the whole Earth's surface, including organic nature.
2) Organic motions repeat unchanged, across individuals side by side and successively within an individual's life or a lineage. This points to a common origin rather than a separate one in each case.
3) Organic arrangements undergo no further development within the life of an individual (men, animals) or of a lineage (plants, embryos). Their cause therefore cannot be a simultaneously running thought-process in that being.

The next page completes the argument. By the same rule (closure, no larger whole, individuality, progressive development), organic purposiveness on Earth is ascribed to a unified, progressing thought-process of the Earth. The Erdseele thus becomes a scientific hypothesis explaining the existence and historical development of the organic world.

The logical skeleton is a conditional inference to the best explanation, with locality conditions (i) and (ii). The conditions are applied twice: first to rule out the organism as the seat, then to rule in the Earth.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. Philosophically, the premise that 'the only explanation of purposiveness is a thought-process' is asserted, not argued.

Reason 3 (no further development of organic arrangements within a lineage) is empirically contestable and sits in tension with the next page's appeal to progressive appearance of ever more perfect organisms, which is development at a larger scale.
Reason 1 does not by itself exclude a distributed or non-mental (e.g. Darwinian) explanation; that exclusion rests entirely on premise (2).

results.what: Analysis of Fechner's Erdseele (Earth-soul) doctrine recast as a hypothesis justified by inductive inference from purposiveness to a unified thought-process, with locality and closure conditions
results.modern_name: Argument from design / inference to the best explanation; panpsychist philosophy of nature (Fechnerian)
results.usually_credited_to: G. T. Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851) for the doctrine; Riemann's critique belongs to his philosophical fragments

deep.surprise_reason: Purely philosophical text on Fechner, whom Riemann is known to have admired. Material of this kind on Fechner and the Erdseele appears in the philosophical fragments printed in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (Naturphilosophie / Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik). There is no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'liegt vielmehr in den Unähnlichkeiten ihr[?] Kraft zu gründen[?]' is doubtful in the image. It may read 'sucht vielmehr auch den Unähnlichkeiten ihre Kraft zu ...'. Uncertain.
'Eingang[?] geben und ersetzen' could be 'Eingang verschaffen und ersetzen'. Uncertain.
After 'Beseeltheit eines Wesens,' there is a struck-out word, probably 'Beseeltheit' or similar.
In point 3, the final 'Zweckmäßigkeit' has a struck or overwritten beginning in the manuscript.
